@jmanico A WebAssembly runtime’s [security model](https://webassembly.org/docs/security/) is very particular. Some offensively oriented papers have been written on it, e.g. [Everything Old is New Again: Binary Security of WebAssembly](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity20/presentation/lehmann). ASVS may mostly focus on verification that when converting to or otherwise adding WebAssembly modules, this model is taken into account.

hi @nielstanis any ideas on this? We are looking for straightforward security recommendations we can use for ASVS related to web assembly.

Design your WebAssembly module in order to avoid exposing functionalities which are not strictly necessary to the WebAssembly module?

This is not very actionnable, though.

Here is my list:

- Verify that all input data passed to WebAssembly modules is thoroughly validated to prevent injection attacks.
- Verify that WebAssembly modules carefully manage memory usage to avoid out-of-bounds memory access and other memory-related vulnerabilities.
- Verify that WebAssembly modules are isolated from the host environment, are run in a sandbox and are granted only the minimum necessary permissions.
- Verify that all communication between WebAssembly modules and the host environment is encrypted and authenticated.

> Verify that WebAssembly modules are isolated from the host environment, are run in a sandbox and are granted only the minimum necessary permissions.

WebAssembly engines are some kind of sandbox already. Do you mean to say:

* "verify that the in-process WebAssembly engine sanboxed the WebAssembly code"
* or "verify that the WebAssembly engine is executed in separate sandbox processes"?

I would not *require* trusted WebAssembly code to be executed in separate (sandbox) **system processes** (but this makes sense to have such a requirement for untrusted user-provided code).

> Verify that all communication between WebAssembly modules and the host environment is encrypted and authenticated.

The "encrypted" part is only useful insofar as the communication is over the network. For authenticated system-level IPC communications (Unix socket), this is not really relevant. I would skip "encrypted" here (because anyway this is already covered by other requirements).

Regarding sandboxing, non-browser environments may benefit from secure WebAssembly runtimes like https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime - very similar to what is built into most browsers.

I **_think_** this is one "verify that the WebAssembly engine is executed in separate sandbox processes"?"

To try to reformulate my previous comment:

> Verify that WebAssembly modules are isolated from the host environment, are run in a **sandbox** and are granted only the minimum necessary permissions.

Do we want to say:

1. system process-level sandbox (eg. based on seccomp BFP, ptrace, Linux namespaces)?
2. any kind of sandbox (possibly only an in-process sandbox such as the one provided by Wasmtime)?

If think we intend to mean (2).

I was wondering whether it was clear enough that the proposed wording means (2) and not (1).

***

> I think this is one "verify that the WebAssembly engine is executed in **separate sandbox processes**"?"

If by "separate sandbox processes", you mean "sandboxed system processes" (1), I don't think the Wasmtime sandbox provides that. The Wasmtime sandbox is an in-process sandbox.

See [Security](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/security.html?highlight=sandbox#security), they talk about everything which is implemented to sandbox the WebAssembly code from the executing system process but nothing is said about:

* executing the code in a separate *system* process;
* sandboxing this process using OS-level sandboxing (seccomp, ptrace, etc.).

In other words, this [code](https://docs.wasmtime.dev/lang-python.html):

~~~python
import wasmtime.loader
import gcd

print("gcd(27, 6) =", gcd.gcd(27, 6))
~~~

does not:

* create new processes (`fork`);
* use seccomp, `ptrace`, namespacess, etc.

There are legitimate cases where you might want to execute WebAssembly **in the same process as the rest of your application**. Wasmtime is supposed to make this safe.
Would you like to propose a PR @randomstuff? I think you get the big picture very well.

I can provide a first draft. Do we intend to have a dedicated chapter for this? V54 WebAssembly?

Disclaimer: the wastime hello world I ran a few comments ago is the first time I have used WebAssembly :)

I feel that a dedicated WebAssembly chapter would be quite short. On the other hand I'm not sure where to move these.

Alternatively, the different requirements might be spread out in the different chapter but I don't think that's desirable.
Do we have enough requirements that are specific to web assembly to make it worthwhile to have a section/chapter for this? Most of the requirements I see above apply to other types of app as well.

> Most of the requirements I see above apply to other types of app as well.

Yes, I agree.

To recap what have been have listed here (with some tweaks).

> Verify that all input data passed to WebAssembly modules is thoroughly validated to prevent injection attacks.

I am wondering if this is much of an issue to deserve a special mention. I would be more wary about data passed by WebAssembly module to the host (which may compromised by some memory corruption in the WebAssembly memory).

> Verify that WebAssembly modules carefully manage memory usage to avoid out-of-bounds memory access and other memory-related vulnerabilities.

This relates to some requirements we have removed in #2280. I would better have a general requirement about memory safety in general and mention WebAssembly modules as an important case.

Anyway, in practice people are going to want to run large pre-existing code base in WebAssembly (think: [Unity](https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.0/Documentation/Manual/wasm-2023-features.html)) and it might be difficult to apply this in practice.

> Verify that all communication between WebAssembly modules and the host environment is encrypted and authenticated.

As discussed earlier I would not include this because it is already covered elsewhere.

> Verify that WebAssembly modules are isolated from the host environment application by the WebAssembly engine. (This includes for example mitigations for Spectre-like vulnerabilities if applicable.)

This could be generalized to other interpreters (eBPF?). This someone amounts to "use a decent WebAssembly implementation", however …

> Verify that the host environment only exposes functionalities to the WebAssembly module which are strictly required for its operation.

For me, this is probably the most important thing we can say about WebAssembly. But then again, this is applicable to other contexts.

So I don't think if we have enough material to have a dedicated section :)
So @randomstuff do think we should close this out and just skip WebAssembly requirements?

Yes, I think we can close this as we don't have much material for a WebAssembly chapter. The question is whether we might want to include some reference to WebAssembly in existing requirements (or chapters).

Might be relevant to revive #2280 into another form? Something like:

> Verify that memory-unsafe code is identified and that a strategy for mitigating binary exploitation is documented according to a risk analysis. This might include hardening compiler flags, isolation of unsafe modules, etc.

About this one:

> Verify that all input data passed to WebAssembly modules is thoroughly validated to prevent injection attacks.

This might be reformulated in the more general case as something like (not a wording proposal):

> Verify that when data flows from a module to a higher-trust module, all input data is thoroughly validated. (For example: untrusted client→trusted server, WebAssembly module→host application, sandboxed environnement executing user code→host application)

Is there such a requirement?  Would there be a need for one?

Ans this one would be related as well to this consideration:

> Verify that the host environment only exposes functionalities to the WebAssembly module which are strictly required for its operation.
